extracted.intended_audience: aspiring journalists, newspaper editors, and readers interested in the profession and standards of journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for the profession of journalism, especially the qualities, duties, and ideals that constitute a successful newspaper editor and trustworthy newspaper. Includes literary-value comments useful for assessing writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great editor qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: "The great editor is by no means the great writer. But he ought to be able to write and must be a judge of writing. The newspaper office is a little kingdom. The great editor needs to know and does know every range of it between the editorial room, the composing room and the pressroom. He must hold well in hand everybody and every function, having risen, as it were, step-by-step from the ground floor to the roof."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrounding guidance: the editor should be conversant with all departments, be a judge of writing, and have risen through the shop so as to manage every function. This is a composite vocational standard rather than a single talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament and practical virtues of an editor
rubrics_metrics.description: "He should be level-headed, yet impressionable; sympathetic, yet self-possessed; able quickly to sift, detect and discriminate; of various knowledge, experience and interest; the cackle of the adjacent barnyard the noise of the world to his eager mind and pliant ear."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance expands: nothing too small or too great for him to tackle; keep to the middle of the road; be adaptable, curious across subjects, decisive in judgment and able to discriminate reliably under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness and integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Disinterestedness being the soul of successful journalism, unselfish devotion to every noble purpose in public and private life, he should say to preferment, as to bribers, 'get behind me, Satan.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an ethical criterion: the editor/journalist must resist bribery and private gain, prioritize public good, and exhibit unselfish devotion. Practical signs include refusing improper preferment and maintaining editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability of personal/one-man journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Personal journalism cannot be escaped, and whether the 'one-man power' emanates from the Counting Room or the Editorial Room, as they are called, it must be clear and answerable, responsive to the common weal, and, above all, trustworthy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a single individual wields editorial power, the rubric demands visible responsibility: clear ownership/accountability, responsiveness to public interest, and trustworthiness. Some jurisdictions legally require a visible responsible presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bennett formula — printing the news fully and fairly
rubrics_metrics.description: "The idea of printing the news of the day, comprising the History of Yesterday, fully and fairly, without fear or favor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historic standard is a journalistic criterion: a newspaper should strive to report the news of the preceding day accurately, fully, and impartially. It is an evaluative rule for what constitutes responsible news reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility as a professional virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: "Assuming journalism, equally with medicine and law, to be a profession, it is the only profession in which versatility is not a disadvantage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike law/medicine where specialization is prized, journalism values breadth. The rubric advises that versatility—ability to work across beats, tasks, and roles—is a positive attribute for journalists and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptitude and stepwise formation of editors
rubrics_metrics.description: "The making of an editor is a complex affair. Poets and painters are said to be born. Editors and orators are made. Many essential elements enter into the editorial fabrication ... Aptitude, as the first ingredient, goes without saying of every line of human endeavor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should consider innate aptitude plus accumulated experience; editors are forged by deliberate cultivation of multiple skills and environment/opportunity. The rubric warns against thinking skill can be entirely manufactured without core aptitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper types and signs of decline
rubrics_metrics.description: "The American newspaper has had ... three separate and distinct epochs; the thick-and-thin, more or less servile party organ; the personal, one-man-controlled, rather blatant and would-be independent; and the timorous, corporation, or family-owned billboard ... Neither its individuality nor its self-exploitation, scarcely its grandiose pretension, remains. There continues to be printed in large type an amount of shallow stuff that would not be missed if it were omitted altogether."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these epochal categories to evaluate a paper's character and health: look for individuality, editorial independence, and substance. A prevalence of "shallow stuff" or over-centralized corporate control are negative indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper's civic role and public discernment
rubrics_metrics.description: "As the world passes from the Rule of Force ... to the Rule of Numbers, the daily journal is destined, if it survives as a power, to become the teacher—the very Bible—of the people. The people are already beginning to distinguish between the wholesome and the meretricious in their newspapers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newspapers on their educative and civic functions: do they inform and elevate public discourse or pander to the meretricious? Public trust and discernment are key outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary-value criteria for assessing writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative judgments about literary figures: e.g., Irving as pioneer and simple vivid writer; Bret Harte's Tales of the Argonauts "exceed the Sketches of Washington Irving alike in wealth of color and humor, in pathos and dramatic action"; "Mark Twain ... did the broadest and strongest work ... nowhere ... the suspicion either of insincerity or of artificiality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use originality, breadth of imagination, sincerity (absence of artifice), wealth of color, humor, pathos, dramatic action, and pioneering influence as criteria when evaluating literary merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about historical 'truth' and source-bias
rubrics_metrics.description: "I wonder shall we ever get any real truth out of what is called history? There are so many sides to it and such a confusing din of voices. How much does old Sam Johnson owe ... to Boswell?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging historical accounts or biographical narratives, apply skepticism: consider source bias, the multiplicity of perspectives, and the shaping role of popular chroniclers (Boswell) before treating an account as 'truth.'
